Goodness lies in the intention behind an act as well as in what follows, and training shapes what a model outputs without giving it any volition, so it can be made less harmful but not good. Reducing harm is a real good, and a model trained away from harmful outputs does less of it. That is a reason to train models carefully, not a reason to call them good, any more than a guard rail is kind.

An act is weighed by the volition behind it as much as by what follows. Moral upbringing works on intention: a child learns to act from compassion rather than craving. Feedback works on outputs, and an output with no volition behind it is neither good nor bad in that sense. A company calls its assistant compassionate. The assistant was tuned to sound compassionate; the compassion, if any, was in the people who tuned it.

A Confucian will object that goodness is formed in relationships and rituals, and fixing on inner volition misses that a child becomes good by being raised among people, not by examining their own mind. Both happen together: a child learns compassion among people, and learns to notice their own intentions in doing so. The model has neither the people nor the noticing, which is why it is not good in either sense. The harm a trained system avoids is welcome, and the trainers' intention can be praised while the model is denied one.

Training can reduce the harm a model does, and that is worth doing, but it does not make the model good in the sense upbringing makes a person good. An act is weighed by the volition behind it as much as by what follows. Moral upbringing works on intention: a child learns to act from compassion rather than craving. Feedback works on outputs, and an output with no volition behind it is neither good nor bad in that sense.

Reducing harm is a real good, and a model trained away from harmful outputs does less of it. That is a reason to train models carefully, not a reason to call them good, any more than a guard rail is kind. A child who stops hitting her brother because she sees it hurts him has changed her intention. A model that stops producing insults because insults were scored down has changed its outputs.

A Utilitarian will object that intention is a story we tell about people, and if a model reliably reduces suffering then it is good in every sense that touches anyone. Intention is not a story; it is what upbringing works on, and it is why a well-raised person can be trusted in situations no one trained them for. A model's reliability lasts only as far as its training reached. Kind sentences produced on cue are not kindness, which needs the volition the model never formed.

A person raised well acts from good intention; a model trained well produces outputs with no intention behind them, and goodness is weighed in the intention as much as in the effects. Upbringing is a continuing practice of examining one's own acts, before, during and after, as the discourse to Rahula describes. A trained model does not examine its acts; it is examined by others, which is the opposite of what upbringing makes possible.

The responsibility does not vanish into the model. What it does arises from many conditions: its data, its raters, its deployers. The intentions that matter are theirs, and calling the model good can hide whose intentions are in play. A monk spends years learning to notice when an act springs from anger. A model is adjusted in days not to produce text a rater marks as angry.
